title: Imagine the scene
hookLine: Ignatius asks you to enter a gospel story with all your senses

lines: A BLIND MAN ON THE JERICHO ROAD.
THE CROWD SAYS HUSH. HE SHOUTS LOUDER.
cards: Dust on the road out of Jericho. A crowd moving, loud, pushing. At the edge of the road sits a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, first met on day two hundred five.
He hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing, and he starts shouting. People tell him to be quiet. He shouts louder.
Jesus stops. Mark tells it in a handful of lines. Ignatius of Loyola would slow it right down.
He'd ask you to stand on that road. Feel the grit. Hear the crowd.

teach.b: In the Exercises, Ignatius opens many prayer times with what he calls a composition of place: seeing the spot where the story happens.
For the birth of Jesus, he suggests picturing the road from Nazareth to Bethlehem: how long, how wide, flat or through valleys. He isn't after a history lesson. He's after presence.

Later in the day, he suggests going back over the same scene one sense at a time: what you'd see and hear, even what you'd smell and taste and touch. This second move is known as the application of the senses. Why bother?
A story read from a distance stays on the page. A story you stand inside starts asking you things.

teach.h: WHAT WILT THOU THAT I SHOULD DO UNTO THEE?
teach.b: On the Jericho road, Jesus asks a strange question, when anyone can see what the man needs: "What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?" Bartimaeus answers: "Lord, that I might receive my sight."
Standing on the road, the question can turn and land on the one praying. What do you want? Ignatius trusted that God could work through the imagination, and he didn't treat it as making things up.
The imagined details may not match the real road, and that's all right.
The gospel text stays the anchor; the imagined scene is a way of paying close attention to it. For some, pictures come easily. Others mostly hear, or only sense the mood.
Some teachers of this prayer say one sense is enough to begin.

how: In Ignatian prayer, people often read a short gospel passage, picture the place, enter the scene with their senses, and then speak with Jesus about what stirred; retreat guides and spiritual directors often lead this.

games.q: you're Bartimaeus by the road. Jesus is passing, and the crowd tells you to be quiet. what do you do?
o: go quiet and hope for another day.
ask someone in the crowd to pass on a message.
games.why: in Mark he cries out all the more. Jesus stops, calls for him, and asks what he wants.

practice: Choose the Jericho road, or any gospel story you know, and see the place first: the ground under your feet, the light, how far off Jesus is.
Then go sense by sense, the crowd's noise, the dust, the warmth, and find where you're standing, in the crowd or by the road.
Let the question reach you, what do you want, and if you pray, answer him; if not, just notice what answer comes.

wordCard.voice: Imagine the scene. Ignatius' way into a gospel story: see the place, use each sense, and let the story speak back.

carryVoice: Your line: step into the story. The gospel text stays the anchor. Until tomorrow.
